question: Object Lifecycle: What is the technical difference in responsibility between new and init when creating a new class instance?

options.text: - new(cls) is the constructor: it allocates the raw memory and returns the newly created instance. - init(self) is the initializer: it accepts the newly allocated instance and configures its attributes.
__new__(cls) initializes attribute values on an already-allocated instance, while __init__(self) is responsible for allocating the raw memory block and returning the object reference.
Both __new__ and __init__ perform the same role; __new__ is simply the legacy Python 2 name for what Python 3 renamed to __init__, kept only for backward compatibility.
__new__(cls) is only invoked for subclasses of built-in immutable types like int or str; ordinary classes skip __new__ entirely and only ever define __init__.

explanation: Specification answer: - new(cls) is the constructor: it allocates the raw memory and returns the newly created instance. - init(self) is the initializer: it accepts the newly allocated instance and configures its attributes.

question: Method Types: When should you use a @classmethod instead of a standard instance method or @staticmethod?

options.text: Use @classmethod when you need access to the class object itself (cls) rather than a specific instance—most commonly to implement alternative factory constructors (e.g., Date.fromtimestamp(ts) or User.fromjson(raw)).
Use @classmethod whenever a method doesn't need self at all; it behaves identically to @staticmethod except that it can also be called on an instance rather than only on the class.
Use @classmethod to guarantee the method runs in a background thread separate from the instance's own thread, which is useful for factory methods that perform I/O.
@classmethod is required any time a method needs to modify self's instance attributes, since instance methods are read-only views of an object's state by default.

explanation: Specification answer: Use @classmethod when you need access to the class object itself (cls) rather than a specific instance—most commonly to implement alternative factory constructors (e.g., Date.fromtimestamp(ts) or User.fromjson(raw)).
